All figures are invented for the exercise and the page says so. hero.text: Two tasks, sixty minutes, and one of them is worth twice as much as the other. Most candidates spend their time the wrong way round.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original RCF English work in the published IELTS Academic Writing format. Not an official IELTS test, and not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.
**All figures in the Task 1 table are invented for this exercise.** They do not describe any real country or any real dataset.

blocks.title: Instructions
text: You have **60 minutes** for both tasks.
Spend about **20 minutes on Task 1** and about **40 minutes on Task 2**. Task 2 is worth **two thirds** of the Writing mark.
Write **at least 150 words** for Task 1 and **at least 250 words** for Task 2. Under-length answers are penalised; there is no upper limit, but very long answers usually contain more errors.
Write in **full sentences**. Notes and bullet points score very low.

blocks.heading: Writing Task 1
text: *You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.*
The table below shows the number of visitors, in thousands, to four types of tourist attraction in one country in 2005, 2012 and 2019.
**Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.**
*Write at least 150 words.*

blocks.heading: Visitors to four types of tourist attraction (thousands)
blocks.caption: Figures invented for this practice task.

blocks.title: What Task 1 is marked on
text: **Task Achievement** - did you give an overview, cover the main features, and report accurately? An answer with no overview paragraph is capped low, however good the English.
**Coherence and Cohesion** - is it organised into paragraphs, and does it flow?
**Lexical Resource** - the range and accuracy of vocabulary.
**Grammatical Range and Accuracy** - the range of structures and how accurately you use them.
Each criterion is worth **25%** of the Task 1 mark. Do not give opinions or reasons in Task 1: there are no marks for explaining *why* the figures moved.

blocks.heading: Writing Task 2
text: *You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.*
Write about the following topic.
*Some people believe that the most effective way to reduce crime is to give longer prison sentences. Others argue that there are better alternatives.*
**Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.**
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.title: What Task 2 is marked on
text: **Task Response** - have you answered the whole question, taken a clear position, and developed your ideas? This instruction has two parts: *discuss both views* **and** *give your own opinion*. An essay that discusses both views and never states an opinion cannot reach Band 7 on this criterion.
**Coherence and Cohesion** - paragraphing and logical progression.
**Lexical Resource** and **Grammatical Range and Accuracy** - as in Task 1.
Each criterion is worth **25%** of the Task 2 mark, and Task 2 is worth **two thirds** of the whole Writing score.

blocks.title: End of the Writing test
text: Model answers for both tasks, with notes on why they score what they score, are on the [answer page](practical-english/ielts/practice-test-1/answers/).
There are ten further Task 2 essays, covering every question type, on the [model essays page](practical-english/ielts/model-essays/).

hero.text: Eleven to fourteen minutes with one examiner, in three parts. The Speaking test is the same for Academic and General Training.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original RCF English work in the published IELTS Speaking format. Not an official IELTS test, and not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: How the Speaking test runs
rows: The examiner checks your identity, then asks questions about yourself and two or three familiar topics.
You are given a card, paper and a pencil. You have 1 minute to prepare, then speak for 1 to 2 minutes. The examiner may ask one or two short follow-up questions.
A two-way discussion of more abstract questions connected to the Part 2 topic.
Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and Pronunciation - each worth 25%.

blocks.heading: Part 1: Introduction and interview
text: *The examiner will ask your name and check your identification, then ask questions on two or three of the following topic sets. Answer in two or three sentences - not one word, and not a speech.*

parts.heading: Your home
bullets: Do you live in a house or an apartment?
What is the room you like most in your home? Why?
Is there anything you would like to change about where you live?
Do you think you will still be living there in five years?

parts.heading: Cooking
bullets: Do you enjoy cooking?
Who does most of the cooking in your home?
Have your eating habits changed in the last few years?
Do you think children should be taught to cook at school? Why?

parts.heading: Weather
bullets: What kind of weather do you like best?
Does the weather affect how you feel?
Is the weather in your country different now from when you were a child?
Do you usually check the forecast?

blocks.heading: Part 2: Long turn
text: *You will have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes if you wish. You then have one to two minutes to speak. Do not start until the examiner tells you to.*

parts.heading: Candidate task card
text: **Describe something practical that an older person taught you.**
You should say:
bullets: who this person was
what they taught you
how they taught it to you
and explain why it has stayed with you.

parts.heading: Follow-up questions the examiner may ask
bullets: Do you still do this now?
Have you ever taught it to anyone else?

blocks.heading: Part 3: Discussion
text: *The examiner will ask further questions connected to the topic of Part 2. These questions are more abstract, and you are expected to give longer, more developed answers.*

parts.heading: Learning from other generations
bullets: What kinds of things are best learned from older people rather than from books or the internet?
Do you think young people today respect the knowledge of older generations as much as they used to?
Why do some practical skills disappear within a single generation?

parts.heading: Skills and society
bullets: Should schools spend more time teaching practical skills? What might they have to give up in order to do so?
Some people say that being able to look anything up has made us worse at remembering things. Do you agree?
How might the skills that are considered valuable change over the next fifty years?

blocks.title: Four things that lift a Speaking band, and one that does not
text: **Extend every answer by one step.** Answer the question, then add a reason, an example or a contrast. Short answers cost fluency marks even when the English is accurate.
**Let yourself be heard thinking.** *That's a difficult one, actually - I suppose it depends on...* is natural speech, and buys time without silence.
**Disagree with the question when you want to.** There are no marks for the opinion itself, and a candidate who says *I'm not sure that's true, actually* usually produces more interesting language.
**Correct yourself once and move on.** Self-correction is credited. Repeatedly restarting the same sentence is not.
**Memorised answers do not work.** Examiners are trained to recognise them, and a rehearsed passage that does not fit the question is treated as evidence that you cannot answer the question.

blocks.title: End of the Speaking test
text: Model answers for all three parts, with notes on what earns the marks, are on the [answer page](practical-english/ielts/practice-test-1/answers/).
